chapters.title: Appendix Four: Preparing the Mind for Combat

assets.topic: Pre-authorizing the response: decisions made before the crisis
assets.visual_frame_description: An old church-hall seminar room at 8 p.m., folding chairs in a horseshoe, a whiteboard reading 'COMBAT PREP: DECIDE NOW.' Rosa Velez, a self-defense teacher, runs a mental-readiness drill for six adults while the player watches from a bench along the wall; each trainee holds a notecard, and a timer ticks beside the board. The player's interface lights up the speech channel, tagging every spoken line as it lands.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the decision-readiness channel: listen to what each trainee says they will do if violence reaches them, and pick the statement that shows a mind already prepared for combat. Identify the cue that separates a pre-authorized response from denial, wishful thinking, and procrastination.
assets.target_channel: Decision-readiness channel: spoken statements revealing whether a person has already decided, in a calm moment, exactly how they will respond to an intrusion or attack.
assets.question: Donna Ferraro, a phlebotomist who parks in a dark hospital ramp at 11 p.m., tells the group how she will handle a stranger who forces his way into her car. Which statement is the strongest cue that Donna has mentally prepared for combat?
assets.correct_cue: Donna says she has decided tonight, not in the moment of crisis: 'If someone gets into my car or grabs me in that ramp, I don't plan to talk, I don't plan to wait to be sure, and I don't plan to fight fair. I'll do whatever it takes to get out and scream until someone comes.' The cue is the specificity and the timing of the decision: a combat-prepared mind settles the response while it is still calm, exactly as this appendix urges, because de Becker's rule is that prediction without preparation is only curiosity. Her decision is concrete about action rather than feelings, and it removes the hesitation that would grant an attacker the advantage.
distractors: I'll stay calm and try to reason with him. Most of these guys just want money, and I'm a good talker.
I try not to think about it, because if I picture it happening I won't sleep for a week.
I've been meaning to sign up for a self-defense class for a while now, and I'll buy pepper spray as soon as I get a chance.
assets.underlying_psychology: The mechanism is pre-decision: a mind that authorizes its own response in advance can act when adrenaline surges, while an undecided mind searches for options in the moment and hesitates. De Becker's case record repeatedly shows victims describing how they saw signals and then waited, stalled, or reasoned in the middle of events; this appendix's answer is to settle the response before the event, converting prediction into preparation rather than curiosity.
key_concepts: De Becker's core rule is that prediction must be followed by preparation; prediction without preparation is just curiosity.
Pre-incident indicators are detectable factors that occur before the outcome being predicted, and the book calls them the single most important tool of prediction.
Denial is the powerful and cunning enemy of successful predictions, filtering out warnings that are close and personal.
When the body perceives danger it prepares physically: blood flows to the arms and legs for fighting or running and cortisol is released to help blood coagulate in case of injury.
Intuition is a survival signal: the mind completes predictions based on experience before conscious logic has finished the work.
Kelly's case shows that a person can receive a clear survival signal and still explain it away because no single visible behavior matched her alarm.
People who commit violence choose their acts from among the options available to them, so predictable behavior is the rule rather than the exception.
Many victims can later point to warnings that were observed but not honored, which is why this appendix presses the reader to settle responses in advance.
Fear is a gift that sharpens attention; the danger is not fear itself but the denial that talks a person out of acting on it.
The decision to act is the difference between being a participant and a spectator in one's own safety, and that decision can be made before the crisis.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests pre-decision as the combat-preparation mechanism: the book insists that prediction without preparation is only curiosity, and this appendix extends that rule by telling the reader to authorize the response before the crisis arrives. The claim is observational rather than experimental, drawn from de Becker's violence-prevention practice in which victims described seeing signals and then hesitating because no response had ever been decided.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: Fear versus worry: which inner voice is a combat-prep signal
assets.visual_frame_description: A 24-hour pharmacy on a winter night, fluorescent lights, one clerk at the register. Omar Reyes, a pharmacy tech, stands behind the counter while a customer in a bulky jacket lingers by the cough-syrup aisle, glancing between the register layout and the exit. A heads-up display floats beside Omar's head, tagging his inner monologue as it ticks by, and the player watches from a security-camera feed in the back office.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the inner-voice channel and separate genuine survival signals from manufactured worry. Listen to Omar's internal commentary and choose the single experience that is a true fear-based signal worth acting on rather than worry.
assets.target_channel: Inner-voice channel: the split between survival-signal fear, which is present-moment, specific, and actionable, and worry, which is future-focused dread the mind manufactures.
assets.question: The customer has been in the store forty minutes with no purchase. Which internal experience of Omar's is a genuine fear signal rather than worry, and thus the one to act on?
assets.correct_cue: The signal to act on is Omar's sudden, present-moment awareness of a specific mismatch: 'His jacket is too heavy for a 67-degree night, he has watched the register layout three times, and he keeps checking the exit. He is not shopping for cough syrup.' The signature of fear worth honoring is that it is about now, it is specific, and it names observable facts; the book defines worry as fear we manufacture about outcomes we cannot reasonably link to the present moment. Combat prep means treating such a signal as information to act on, by stepping back, calling the manager, or preparing a response, rather than explaining it away.
distractors: What if my car doesn't start tonight and I get stranded on the way home?
I should have studied harder for my license renewal; what if I fail it again next month?
I feel generally on edge tonight and probably shouldn't have skipped dinner.
assets.underlying_psychology: This tests the fear-versus-worry distinction: fear is the mind completing a prediction about the present, while worry is self-generated dread about the future and is a form of self-harassment. The book's argument is that accurate fear is a survival gift that names real hazards, and the mental preparation this appendix describes depends on telling the two apart so that true signals are neither wasted nor ignored.
key_concepts: Worry is the fear we manufacture: it is about dreaded outcomes we cannot reasonably link to the present moment, and worrying is a form of self-harassment.
Fear, by contrast, is a survival signal tied to present conditions and is a gift that tells the truth about danger.
Intuition is listening: the mind picks up observable details and completes predictions before conscious logic can.
Survival signals are often carried by small, specific inconsistencies rather than dramatic gestures.
Denial persuades people to discard signals they cannot explain, because the voice of denial whispers that nothing is wrong.
Goleman's account describes worrying as a sort of magical amulet some people feel wards off danger.
A prepared person has already decided which signals matter and which responses they will use.
Alarming words can put people into a defensive posture psychologically even without real risk, while true signals point to real risk.
Most violence is preceded by detectable signals, so the well-trained ear treats sudden present-moment alarm as information.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the fear-versus-worry distinction, the mechanism by which survival signals get either honored or discarded: fear is present-moment and specific, worry is manufactured dread about the future. De Becker argues on the basis of his case practice that true fear is a gift that can be trusted to name real hazards, and that worry wastes the attention the prepared mind needs for real signals.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: The post-incident audit: was the mind prepared or in denial?
assets.question: After an attempted carjacking in the Cedar Hills mall garage, Raj Bedi tells his story to a counselor. Was Raj's mind prepared for combat, in denial, or something else, and what does his account reveal about preparation?
assets.subject_baseline: Raj Bedi, 34, is a railway-signal engineer who prides himself on methodical thinking. Colleagues describe him as calm under pressure and unemotional; he jokes that feelings are for the weekend. He has never taken a self-defense class, has no variation in his commute apart from the same route every day, and on a pre-visit questionnaire wrote that thinking about crime makes him uncomfortable, so he doesn't.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 0:00-0:06: Raj recounts arriving at garage level P2 and seeing a man in a dark hoodie leaning on the car two spaces from his own, watching him. 0:07-0:11: He says he noticed him early, maybe ninety seconds, but decided he was probably waiting for someone; his hands are clasped and his voice measured. 0:12-0:19: He describes the man stepping toward him, and for the first time his gaze drops; he says he couldn't get the key in the door, then adds quickly that it was dark. 0:20-0:26: Asked whether he considered honking, driving out, or calling anyone, he laughs briefly, shakes his head, and says he didn't want to make a scene over nothing. 0:27-0:33: He concludes that the man was just a scared kid, that he handled it fine, and that he doesn't believe in all that gut stuff.
assets.interrogation_transcript: COUNSELOR: 'You saw him before he reached you?' RAJ: 'Sixty, ninety seconds. He was just leaning there. I told myself he was waiting for somebody.' COUNSELOR: 'What did you feel when he started walking toward you?' RAJ: 'I don't... I knew the door lock. I fumbled it. It was dark.' COUNSELOR: 'Did you use the horn? Reverse? Your phone?' RAJ: '(laughs) That's not how I'm built. I didn't want to make a scene over nothing.' COUNSELOR: 'What do you make of it now?' RAJ: 'I handled it fine. He was just a kid. I don't believe in all that gut stuff.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Raj's mind was not prepared, and his account is a textbook performance of denial after the fact. He recorded a genuine pre-incident signal, ninety seconds of a stranger surveilling him in an empty garage, but he had never authorized a response in advance, so he substituted a story (he was waiting for someone), froze at the door, complied, and now minimizes the event (just a kid, I handled it fine, I don't believe in all that gut stuff). The audit shows the unprepared mind doing exactly what this appendix warns against: translating a survival signal into nothing.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: (1) Baseline: Raj has declared that he does not think about crime and has no response plan, which means his fear system would have to invent a response mid-event. (2) The log shows a signal detected and then discarded: he saw the man ninety seconds early, a pre-incident indicator, and actively explained it away rather than acting on it, the signature of denial filtering out a close, personal threat. (3) The physical detail (couldn't get the key in the door) betrays the freeze that follows an undecided mind under adrenaline, and his quick add-on that it was dark is an attempt to manage the interviewer's impression. (4) The transcript's dismissal of all that gut stuff is the book's denial in one phrase: intuition is the mechanism that would have told him to reverse the car the moment he saw the watcher. Verdict: unprepared and in denial. He is not lying about the events; he is actively misreading them, and the danger is that a man who has survived once by luck will describe luck as skill.
distractors: Prepared and calm: he kept his composure, complied to minimize harm, and correctly read the man as a non-threatening kid.
Post-traumatic exaggeration: he is embellishing the attention he gave the man to impress the counselor with his awareness.
Deliberate deception to obtain a defensive-driving reclassification and lower insurance rates.
key_concepts: The book defines denial as the powerful and cunning enemy of successful predictions, and its signature is filtering out warnings that are close and personal.
Pre-incident indicators are detectable factors that occur before the outcome being predicted, and the man's presence in the garage was one of them.
Kelly's story shows a person receiving a survival signal and discarding it because no single visible behavior explained her alarm.
Prediction without preparation is just curiosity, and the cost is paid in hesitation at the moment of action.
Preparing the mind for combat means deciding the response in a calm hour, so adrenaline does not have to invent one.
The physiological fear response mobilizes the body for action, blood to the limbs and cortisol for clotting, and the undecided mind wastes that mobilization in a freeze.
Intuition is listening, and the people who reverse out of a garage for no reason are honoring what they heard.
Violence is rarely random: the attacker's approach followed a sequence the observer could see.
A story that turns one's own survival into luck and dismisses the signal as gut stuff is the audit trail of an unprepared mind, not a calm one.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests denial and the lack of a pre-authorized response: a man who detected a pre-incident indicator and explained it away, then froze, then reframed luck as competence. These are de Becker's observational findings from his prediction practice rather than experimental results, and the appendix's prescription, decide the response before the crisis, is a case-based recommendation.
assets.visual_frame_description: A windowless counseling room with a voice recorder and a stack of intake forms. Raj Bedi sits across from the counselor, recounting the attempted carjacking in the Cedar Hills mall garage, and the player watches through a one-way mirror as his words are transcribed live onto the screen. Timestamped tags appear beside each statement, marking where his account shifts from description to explanation.
assets.player_mission: Audit Raj's full account of the attempted carjacking and decide whether his mind was prepared for combat, in denial, or something else. Compare his baseline habits, the timed observations, and the interview transcript, then deliver the verdict with the evidence.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

chapters.title: Appendix Five: Gavin de Becker & Associates

assets.topic: The intake audit: real assessment case or nuisance mail?
assets.question: Dana Whitfield, chief of staff to State Senator Lena Ortiz, brings a stack of letters from a constituent named Carl Prentiss and asks whether it is a case worth assessing. Is this a legitimate threat-assessment referral, a nuisance, or something else?
assets.subject_baseline: Dana Whitfield is precise and low-drama: in three years as chief of staff she has never made a security referral, and staff describe her as someone who finishes paperwork before gossip. She opens the conversation by handing over a neatly tabbed folder and asks what standard the assessment team applies, rather than telling them what to think.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 0:00-0:10: Dana places the folder on the table and says the letters started seven months ago, thirty-one of them so far; her voice is flat and she reads the count from a sticky note she has kept for weeks. 0:11-0:25: Asked what the letters contain, she flips through tabs describing the sequence: early letters addressed to Senator Ortiz, later ones to Lena, and the last four signed your own family waiting to be reunited. 0:26-0:38: She recounts that Prentiss has twice appeared in the district office lobby asking for special access because he is practically family; her hands stay still, but she corrects the interviewer's word bother to appear. 0:39-0:52: Asked whether she feels afraid, she pauses and answers that she doesn't have to feel afraid for it to be a case, and that is why she brought the letters in.
assets.interrogation_transcript: ANALYST: 'What was in the first letters?' DANA: 'Respectful complaints about a highways bill. Addressed to Senator Ortiz, full title. I answered them myself.' ANALYST: 'And the most recent?' DANA: 'Addressed to Lena. Talking about our wedding, our children, our life. He writes that we already know each other, that the senator just doesn't remember yet.' ANALYST: 'Has he ever made a threat?' DANA: 'No. He has never threatened her. He talks as though they are already married. I brought him to you because this looks like the delusions-of-identity pattern, not a grouch with a complaint.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Legitimate threat-assessment referral. The letters' trajectory, from formal titles to first name to a claimed marriage and family, is the imagined-intimacy pattern the book tracks in cases against public figures, and the writer's physical appearances at the office show the pursuit moving from mail to access. The case deserves assessment, not dismissal: the practice described in this appendix is built on monitoring exactly such progressions, including a fifteen-year monitoring file on a stalker of a public figure.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: (1) Baseline: Dana's record of never making referrals and her tabbed, dated folder show a witness who is careful rather than excitable, giving the evidence weight. (2) The log's key turn is the correspondence shift itself: formal address to first name to wedding, children, our life, the escalation of claimed relationship that the book associates with delusions of identity (DEL-ID, and the SPOUSE-DEL variant for those claiming marriage to a client). (3) The appearances in the lobby add an access-seeking dimension, since stalking is how would-be attackers attain the intimacy with a target they cannot get any other way. (4) Her correction of bother to appear and her final line, that evidence does not need her fear to be valid, show she has separated the signal from her own comfort. Verdict: a case file in the making, to be monitored with the same discipline the firm applies to mailed obsession, not dismissed as nuisance mail.
distractors: Nuisance mail: a lonely constituent venting about highways legislation, best answered with a form letter.
Personal vendetta: Dana is using security protocols to punish a constituent who embarrassed her earlier in a public meeting.
Panic from an over-vigilant staffer: Dana read the book and is now seeing stalkers in ordinary constituent mail.
key_concepts: The firm described in this appendix monitors cases over years; de Becker's office kept a fifteen-year monitoring file on a stalker of a public figure.
In evaluating cases the practice considers a hundred and fifty pre-incident indicators beyond those commonly discussed.
Through stalking, would-be attackers come to know their victims more closely than they know others in their lives.
Cases in which people believe they are married to one of the clients are classified SPOUSE-DEL, a delusion-of-identity category the office tracks.
The assumption that a person who makes no explicit threat is harmless is not supported by the practice's case record.
By the time an incident happens, the letters and the appearances were there to be read; the book's method is reading them.
Escalation in correspondence from formal titles to first names to claimed family is a documented pattern in obsession cases.
Physical presence seeking access is a more advanced stage than writing letters, because it moves the writer into the victim's real space.
The appendix presents the firm's standards as rigorous assessment, separating a referral from drama so that warnings are respected.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the imagined-intimacy progression: correspondence evolving from formal address to claimed relationship and physical access-seeking, the pattern the firm in this appendix was organized to track. The categories (DEL-ID, SPOUSE-DEL) and the fifteen-year monitoring practice come from de Becker's case work with public figures, an observational and case-based record rather than a controlled study.
assets.visual_frame_description: A clean intake office at a threat-assessment firm, a folder of thirty-one letters spread on a gray table. Dana Whitfield sits opposite the analyst, and the letters are arrayed by date so the player can watch the salutations march from Senator Ortiz to Lena to our wedding. A replay control lets the player return to her corrections of wording.
assets.player_mission: Audit Dana Whitfield's referral and decide whether Carl Prentiss is a legitimate threat-assessment case or a nuisance. Compare her baseline reliability, the timed observations of how she presents the evidence, and the interview transcript, then issue the intake verdict.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: The escalation memo: weighing the indicators before raising protection
assets.question: Senior analyst Nedra Whitfield reviews a file on Jesse Compton, who has been writing to Superior Court Judge Amara Voss for nine months, and must decide whether to raise the judge's protection level to continuous coverage. Should the team escalate?
assets.subject_baseline: Nedra Whitfield has run the assessment desk for eleven years and is known for memorizing case law and resisting team drama; junior analysts joke that she only gets excited about footnotes. The standing rule she enforces is that no single angry letter justifies round-the-clock protection, and neither does the lack of an explicit threat clear a case.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 0:00-0:15: Nedra opens the binder: nine months of letters with a frequency graph showing acceleration from one letter a month to eleven in the final month; her pencil ticks the chart and her face shows nothing. 0:16-0:30: She reads aloud the shifting salutation, 'Your Honor' giving way to 'Darling,' and the recent line about the court that united them soon recognizing what they agreed to in private; she underlines agreed to in private. 0:31-0:45: A second graph shows the writer's gas receipts and phone records: trips to the county where the judge sits on days she presides, including a visit to the courthouse lobby two weeks ago; she taps the line labeled random travel. 0:46-0:58: She closes the binder and notes that the writer's only criminal record is a decade-old traffic violation, adding that there is no history of violence, and that is exactly why the file is dangerous to misread.
assets.interrogation_transcript: JUNIOR ANALYST: 'No threats, no record, no violence. Shouldn't we hold at the current level?' NEDRA: 'The record is the least informative page in this binder. Look at page eleven: he writes that the judge is his wife. That is the delusion-of-identity indicator, and it is the one we would want to know above all others.' JUNIOR ANALYST: 'But he has never done anything.' NEDRA: 'He has done everything on paper, and then he moved to her county and stood in her courthouse lobby. The mail was the rehearsal. The indicators are converging.' JUNIOR ANALYST: 'So we go to continuous coverage?' NEDRA: 'We go to continuous coverage, and we tell the judge exactly why, so she can help us with her own eyes.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Escalate to continuous coverage. The file shows the indicators converging: accelerating volume and a shift into imagined intimacy (agreed to in private), grandiosity in the writer's self-portrayal as co-author of the court, random travel and physical proximity to the judge's workplace, and the absence of any criminal history that might have flagged him earlier, which makes the quiet escalation harder to see. The team's stated priority is the delusion-of-identity indicator, the PIN above all others, and the pattern warrants the higher protection level.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: (1) Baseline: Nedra's enforcement of the two standing rules shows the decision is being made against the proper standard: no panic inflation, no false clear. (2) The log shows the analyst reading the documented indicators: volume and frequency acceleration, the salutation shift into a claimed private agreement (imagined relationship), travel into the judge's county and courthouse (physical approach), and grandiosity in the self-description. (3) The negative indicator, no criminal record, is correctly weighed: the book's cases show that dangerous people often look and act like anyone else, and monitoring is about behavior, not records. (4) The transcript's final beat is the appendix's discipline: the recommendation is made and the judge is informed so that her own perception adds to the protection. Verdict: escalate, and treat the correspondence as the rehearsal it is.
distractors: Hold at the current level, because the only hard evidence is letters and no explicit threat has been made.
Escalate merely because a judge is involved, since judicial office always requires the highest protection by policy.
Close the case: a decade-old traffic record and no history of violence prove the writer is not a danger.
key_concepts: The practice evaluates a hundred and fifty pre-incident indicators beyond the commonly discussed list.
When asked to choose one PIN above all others, the firm points to the delusion-of-identity indicator: belief in a relationship that does not exist.
Categories such as DEL-ID and SPOUSE-DEL organize cases in which subjects believe they are the Messiah, a celebrity, or married to a client.
Displayed grandiosity and narcissism are among the indicators assessed in cases against public figures.
Random or otherwise unexplained travel is one of the listed indicators evaluated by the practice.
Identifying with a stalker or assassin is another listed indicator in the assessment of potential attackers.
The absence of a criminal record or a history of violence does not clear a case, because violent people often look and act like anyone else.
Stalking is how would-be attackers achieve the intimacy with a target they could not otherwise reach.
Monitoring is a long game: de Becker's office tracked one stalker of a public figure for fifteen years before the picture resolved.
Informing the protected person is part of protection: the judge's own informed attention is treated as a layer of defense.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the convergence of pre-incident indicators, accelerating mail, imagined intimacy, travel toward the target, and grandiosity, weighed against a clean record that invites false comfort. The hundred-and-fifty-indicator practice and the delusion-of-identity priority are de Becker's case-based standards from his threat-assessment firm, observational expertise rather than validated psychometrics.
assets.visual_frame_description: A fluorescent document-review room where Nedra Whitfield works through the Compton binder in silence, her pencil producing a frequency graph as the months accelerate. Above the table, the player sees the case's key exhibits highlighted: the salutation shift, the gas receipts, and the courthouse-lobby visit, each tagged with the indicator it corresponds to.
assets.player_mission: Audit the analyst's escalation decision on the Compton file and judge whether continuous coverage is warranted. Weigh the converging indicators against the clean record, read the timed review and the team exchange, then confirm or overturn the recommendation.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: The entitlement channel: reading the letter stream for imagined relationship
assets.visual_frame_description: A quiet corner of a TV-station newsroom at 2 a.m., where analyst Priya Anand scrolls a nine-month archive of letters to anchor Richard Okada. Each letter appears as a date-stamped card, and the player's cursor is a magnifier that highlights pronoun shifts while Priya narrates the sequence aloud. A wall clock counts the months and a small graph tracks the writer's references to we and us.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the entitlement channel of the correspondence and identify the single shift that most strongly signals the writer is moving from admiration toward action. Read the letter stream and choose the detail a threat-assessment analyst would flag first.
assets.target_channel: Entitlement channel: language markers in correspondence that reveal the writer's claimed relationship with the target, from formal viewer to imagined intimate.
assets.question: The letter stream to anchor Richard Okada began with viewer praise and autograph requests. Which single shift in the correspondence is the strongest cue that the writer has crossed into the delusion-of-identity territory the firm monitors?
assets.correct_cue: The strongest cue is the pronoun shift at month six, when the writer stops describing Okada's life and starts describing a shared one: 'I watch you every night' becomes 'We have built something rare in this city, and the night is coming when the audience will know about us, and my mother has already set a place for you at our table.' Claiming a family role and a public destiny with the target is the imagined-relationship marker, the delusion-of-identity PIN the office would want to know above all others, and it means the writer now experiences Okada's life as something he is entitled to enter rather than watch.
distractors: An early letter demanding that the station correct an on-air mispronunciation of the writer's hometown.
A single angry letter calling Okada a tool of the network for dropping a story.
An autograph request with a pre-addressed stamped envelope, which most viewers consider ordinary.
assets.underlying_psychology: This tests imagined intimacy as a pre-incident indicator: the mechanism by which an admirer converts the target's public life into a private relationship in the writer's own mind. De Becker's case record shows would-be attackers attaining their greatest intimacy with targets through stalking and correspondence, and the firm's classification system (DEL-ID, SPOUSE-DEL) exists because this belief, not anger, is what precedes action in many cases.
key_concepts: Among the firm's categories are DEL-ID cases, in which people believe they are the Messiah, Captain Kirk, or Marilyn Monroe.
SPOUSE-DEL classifies subjects who believe they are married to one of the firm's clients.
The delusion-of-identity indicator is the single PIN the practice would want to be aware of above all others.
Through stalking and correspondence, would-be attackers come to know their victims far more closely than the victims know them.
The greatest intimacy most would-be attackers attain with public figures is built from the outside, through watching and writing.
Attack cases show that the assailant's imagined relationship with the target is a central feature of the fixation.
Escalating we-language in correspondence is a detectable move from observer to participant in the writer's own mind.
A lack of explicit threats in the letters does not reduce the level of concern.
The assessment method evaluates the trajectory of the relationship the writer claims, not just the content of each letter.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the imagined-relationship escalation embedded in correspondence: pronoun and entitlement markers that show a writer converting a public figure into a private partner. The DEL-ID and SPOUSE-DEL categories, and the claim that delusion-of-identity is the indicator the firm would most want to know, come from de Becker's case-based classification system in a field with minimal experimental validation.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

chapters.title: Appendix Six: The Elements of Prediction

assets.topic: The context channel: relationship of parties before contact
assets.visual_frame_description: A tidy apartment lobby at dusk: Ruth Okonkwo, a nurse who recently testified in a high-profile trial, walks in with groceries. At the mailboxes, a courier in a generic green vest is coincidentally sorting a bundle for the building across the street while watching the elevators. A heads-up display tracks his route, his timing, and his small talk, and a clipboard on the concierge desk holds Ruth's delivery schedule.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the context channel, the relationship between the courier and Ruth's routine, and identify the single observation that most strongly predicts contact. Choose the cue an analyst would weigh under the elements of prediction.
assets.target_channel: Context channel: the relationship of parties and events, how a person's timing, route, and small talk connect them to the target's routine and access.
assets.question: For three weeks the courier has arrived in Ruth's lobby within minutes of her return from shift. Which single observation is the strongest element-of-prediction signal that this is more than friendly coincidence?
assets.correct_cue: The decisive cue is that his arrivals synchronize with her schedule while his stated errand is for other buildings: at 6:12 p.m. on each of her three shift nights he appears sorting parcels for the building across the street, mentions that the mailroom code was changed but he remembers it anyway, and asks the concierge which floor the new resident on the news lives on. The elements of prediction put weight on the relationship between the parties and events: his behavior is organized around her times and her identity, not around his stated purpose, and he is cultivating knowledge of her access. Context is the frame that turns an ordinary errand into a pattern.
distractors: He delivers parcels for the building across the street on a fixed route that happens to pass this lobby.
He greets Ruth by name one day, having learned it from the mailbox labels like other couriers do.
He once mentioned that his sister works at the same hospital as Ruth, offering a plausible social link.
assets.underlying_psychology: This tests the relationship-of-parties element: the meaning of a behavior changes with its context, so an errand that repeats in synchrony with the target's routine and includes curiosity about her identity is a different behavior from the same errand without the pattern. De Becker's method holds that the context of parties and events is a core element of prediction, because violence and contact announce themselves more in pattern than in any single gesture.
key_concepts: A core element of prediction is the relationship of parties and events to each other.
A person's contribution to risk includes accessibility: setting, circumstance, and how available one makes oneself to a criminal.
Pre-incident indicators are detectable factors that occur before the outcome being predicted.
The book's model asks what the parties' connection is before asking whether any single act is threatening.
Behavior that is not normally threatening can become alarming when placed in an uninvited context.
Most violence follows a sequence a careful observer can see, not a random strike.
People who plan contact with a target frequently rehearse through coincidental presence, and the pattern is the signal.
The difference between friendliness and surveillance is the relationship of the timing to the target's life.
Prediction depends on gathering the same details intuition processes: sequence, timing, and connection.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the relationship-of-parties element: the context channel that determines whether a repeated errand is a routine delivery or coordinated contact. The book's claim, that events and people take their meaning from their relationship to the target and that this is one of the elements of prediction, is case-derived reasoning rather than a controlled finding.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: The exit interview audit: applying the elements before the termination
assets.question: Midland Industrial's HR director, Collette Rinehart, conducts the termination of machinist Ray Delgado after a documented safety violation and must judge whether the exit conversation signals future danger. Does Ray's conduct require a protection plan?
assets.subject_baseline: Collette Rinehart has run HR at the plant for nine years and has terminated more than a hundred employees, mostly without incident. She is methodical: compensation owed, badge and keys, a scripted exit, witnesses in the room. She has read the company guidance on workplace violence and believes threats are usually preceded by observable warnings that supervisors should log.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 0:00-0:12: Ray sits down, arms folded, and listens to the termination letter without reacting; he nods once at the mention of the safety-committee hearing. 0:13-0:25: Told he is released today, he leans forward and says this is a war now and he has never lost a war, with a flat smile; his palms stay on the table and the smile does not reach his eyes. 0:26-0:38: Asked about his next step, he says he will make them pay for this and that their whole management family will remember his name; he then taps the folder with Collette's home address in it and says it is all in there anyway. 0:39-0:52: To the witness he adds that they should not worry about him, because he knows exactly where everyone sits; he leaves without asking about severance.
assets.interrogation_transcript: RINEHART: 'Ray, the decision is final. Your last check clears Friday.' RAY: 'This is a war now, and I've never lost a war.' RINEHART: 'We'll help you transition. References, counseling.' RAY: 'I'll make them pay for this. Your whole management family will remember my name.' (taps the folder containing his own HR file, which carries the office map) RINEHART: 'Ray, let's keep this productive.' RAY: 'Don't worry about me. I know exactly where everyone sits. I'll see you around the parking lot, Collette.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Escalation signals requiring an immediate protection plan. The exit conversation shows the pattern the book describes before workplace violence: the grievance framed as a war with the employer as enemy, the reference to management family, and the shift from vague anger to specific personal knowledge (your home address in this file, where everyone sits, the parking lot, Collette). The nominal calm, no scream and no overt kill-you phrasing, is not reassurance; the specificity is the escalation.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: (1) Baseline: Collette's history of uneventful terminations establishes that most exits are angry but contain no escalation, giving this one diagnostic weight. (2) The log isolates the signatures: the war framing (never lost a war) is the grievance language the book's workplace chapter flags, and the dead-eyed smile with still palms is a calm overlay, not the man's baseline. (3) The turn to personal addresses and seating knowledge moves the anger from the job to the people, which is the escalation from manipulation, words meant to influence an outcome, toward action. (4) The elements of prediction converge with the history of the parties: Ray once told a supervisor he would be hearing from him for years after a write-up, and the grievance and unreasonable-expectation indicators are present. Verdict: log it, brief security, watch the parking perimeter, and do not negotiate or offer reassurance next week; contact with a man who says he will see you in the parking lot is fuel.
distractors: Normal termination anger: most fired employees are upset, and Ray left without violence.
Cry-for-help behavior: Ray wants attention and an apology, and a follow-up conversation next week will resolve it.
Deliberate theatrical threat for leverage in a wrongful-termination claim, best answered with a counter-intimidation letter from counsel.
key_concepts: The book links the fired employee's rage to losses: loss of status, income, security, purpose, identity, and above all loss in a fight.
Manipulations are statements intended to influence an outcome without resorting to threat; escalations are actions intended to cause fear.
Warning signs in the workplace are usually observable by several people, yet they are frequently ignored.
Unreasonable expectations, elevation, an apology, or being named the winner in some dispute, figure among the workplace indicators of risk.
Grievance framed as an institutionalized war is a documented feature in workplace-violence files.
After a termination decision, the golden rule is do not negotiate; further discussion feeds the relationship.
Anger is such a risk factor that it supersedes even smoking, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol in de Becker's account of hostile people.
Among the elements of prediction, the relationship of the parties and the history of their interactions carry weight.
The absence of an explicit I-will-kill-you does not clear a case; the book warns that obvious warnings are frequently ignored because they are not dramatic.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the workplace escalation pattern: grievance language, personal targeting, and the convergence of relationship history with pre-incident indicators during a termination. The patterns come from de Becker's workplace-violence cases and the indicator list in his occupational-hazards chapter, observational expertise rather than a validated scale.
assets.visual_frame_description: A conference room in the Midland Industrial plant with a laminated safety poster on the wall, an HR file open on the table, and a witness seated at the far end. Ray Delgado sits opposite Collette Rinehart as the termination letter is read, and the player sees the conversation transcript tagged with timestamps and gesture notes in the margin.
assets.player_mission: Audit the termination meeting between Collette Rinehart and Ray Delgado and decide whether the exit conversation requires a protection plan. Compare his baseline, the timed nonverbal log, and the transcript, then deliver the workplace-violence verdict with the evidence.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: The predictive-circle gauntlet: weighing a suitor against the elements
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The boss battle tests the full set of elements in one case: the relationship between the parties, the subject's behavior history and pre-incident indicators, the predictive circle for intimate violence, and the emotional-leverage persuasion the book prescribes. The player must first read the observations correctly, placing a new boyfriend against the documented indicators for spousal-killing risk, and then choose an intervention that works on the emotional reality of the woman at risk rather than on logic and statistics.
assets.stage_1_observation: Nadia Osorio, a 41-year-old accountant, introduces her new boyfriend, Tyler Vonn, at her sister Mara's dinner party. The player sits across the room and watches: Tyler steers Nadia away from the fire escape and corner windows, telling her to save those seats for them, then walks her car and her house perimeter before leaving, explaining that he likes to know the exits of every place she visits. Later, Nadia tells Mara that Tyler has gone through her phone twice for her own safety, has her work schedule memorized, and last week threatened to find whoever whistled at her at a bus stop, then brought her flowers and cried, promising he only does it because he loves her. Mara laughs it off as dramatic but devoted. The player reads the evening's transcript with the book's predictive list open beside it.
assets.stage_1_question: Which single observation in the evening places Tyler closest to the center of the predictive circle for intimate homicide?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The combination of control and contrition, phone surveillance for her own safety, memorized schedules, threatening a stranger over a whistle, then weeping with flowers, is the pattern the book places near the center of the predictive circle: a boyfriend who monitors, bullies, threatens, and then delivers the apology that keeps her attached. The most chilling detail is that he is already casing her exits, and when a man resolves conflict with intimidation and then rewards the woman with tenderness, both behaviors are instruments of control rather than separate moods. Mara's dramatic-but-devoted reframe is precisely the denial that lets the pattern advance.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Six weeks later Nadia calls Mara in tears: Tyler has moved into her apartment, quit his job so that nothing gets between them, and punched a hole in the bathroom door when she mentioned a business trip. He is now calling her ten times an hour at the office, and she says she is sure he would never hurt her, he just gets scared. Mara asks the player what to do tonight. Choose the intervention.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Do not argue with Nadia about statistics, and do not tell her to just leave him: the book's case record shows that leaving is the most dangerous moment and that logic rarely moves a battered woman. Instead, ask about her fear directly and honor it, help her build a safety plan with a battered women's program (a shelter referral, a code word, a packed bag, someone designated to care for the children or pets), and build the plan for the possibility of leaving so it exists before it is needed. Refuse to meet Tyler or negotiate with him, because do-not-negotiate is the rule with people who will not let go, and make the first call tonight: the escalating phone barrage and the hole in the door are the signals, not the apology. The intervention that works is emotional leverage, standing with her fear and giving her a concrete path, not a lecture.
key_concepts: A man who resolves conflict with intimidation, bullying, and violence is among the predictive factors the book lists for intimate violence.
Verbal abuse and the use of threats as instruments of control are listed among the predictive factors.
A boyfriend who has threatened the woman, terrorized her, and stalked her sits very near the center of the predictive circle for wife murder.
Though these men are frequently kind and gentle in the beginning, there are always warning signs; victims may not always choose to detect them.
Though leaving is the best response to violence, it is in trying to leave that most women get killed.
Persuading a battered woman requires emotional leverage, not statistics or moral arguments.
Restraining orders remain what author Linden Gross calls law enforcement's knee-jerk response, a single tool rather than a plan.
The threatened woman's own fear is the most reliable indicator in the file, and the man who apologizes and cries after frightening her is still using fear as control.
The book lists designating someone to care for children among the practical elements of a safety plan.
Do not negotiate is the golden rule for getting out of any relationship with a person who refuses to let go.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the predictive-circle method: placing a controlling, threatening suitor against the documented indicators for intimate homicide, then acting on the insight that leaving is the most dangerous phase and that persuasion requires emotional leverage. The predictive factors are de Becker's case-derived list for what he calls America's most predictable murders, observational expertise about spousal violence.
assets.visual_frame_description: A dinner party recreated in holographic replay: Tyler Vonn steering Nadia Osorio away from windows, circling her car, and later kneeling with flowers beside a torn-up phone. To the player's left floats the book's predictive list for intimate violence, each item lighting up as the evening's evidence touches it, and Mara's laughter echoes through the replay loop.
assets.player_mission: Read the evening's replay against the elements of prediction and place Tyler on the predictive circle for intimate homicide, then take Mara's call six weeks later and choose the intervention that works on Nadia's emotional reality rather than on logic.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

chapters.title: Appendix Seven: Questions For Your Child's School

assets.topic: The school-response channel: honoring or explaining away a student threat
assets.visual_frame_description: Jefferson Middle School's front office on a Thursday afternoon. A parent, Greg Tan, sits across from Assistant Principal Darla Oberman after his 13-year-old son found a note in his locker signed by a classmate named Kevin, reading that the school will hear from him after Friday. On the wall behind Darla hangs the school's crisis binder, and a tablet on the desk shows its incident log; two floating panels display the school's written response and the boy's file.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the school's response channel and decide which reaction is the strongest evidence that the school treats warning signs as information rather than as noise. Choose the response that matches the book's prediction posture.
assets.target_channel: School-response channel: what the institution does with a threat report, log, assess, notify, and act versus reassure, minimize, and deflect.
assets.question: Greg's son found the threat in his locker, and the note-writer is a classmate named Kevin. Which school response is the strongest cue that Jefferson is prepared to predict rather than deny?
assets.correct_cue: The prepared response is a documented chain: Kevin's note is logged as an incident, two witnesses are interviewed privately (one reports that Kevin has been drawing scenes of children on fire and talking nonstop about the news reports of the recent school attack), Greg's son is moved to a supervised class for the week, both sets of parents are called, and the resource officer opens a threat-assessment review for Friday. The cue is that the school treats the note as information to investigate, with witnesses, context, and a review, rather than as a moment to reassure anyone. De Becker's method is that warning signs are detectable before events, and the denial reflex, he is just venting, he would never do it, is what must be overcome.
distractors: The school reassures Greg that the note is typical middle-school drama and that boys often write scary things they never mean.
The school calls both boys to the office, makes Kevin apologize in front of the counselor, and declares the matter resolved with a handshake.
The school announces it has hired two new security guards and installed a metal detector so incidents like this can't happen.
assets.underlying_psychology: This tests institutional denial versus prediction: the reflex to label ominous signals as drama or to answer warnings with visible security theater (guards, detectors) instead of investigation. De Becker documents that warning signs are usually observable by several people yet frequently ignored, and that hiring guards without training is a common false resolution; the prepared institution logs, interviews, and reviews.
key_concepts: Campus violence is typically preceded by observable warning signs, yet officials often describe the perpetrator afterward as a quiet or star student.
The book names a perpetrator's fascination with violent media among the warning signs that precede mass-casualty incidents.
When organizations are pressured to improve security, the typical response is to hire guards, but guards without training or supervision only create the feeling that the matter has been addressed.
Threats and warning signs sit in the open where several people are in a position to observe them.
Treating a written threat as information to investigate, with witnesses and a review, follows the prediction posture.
Denial is the enemy of successful predictions, whispering that the threatening boy doesn't look the part.
Violence, like any behavior, has a purpose, and threats are among the instruments by which a young person tests for status.
Resolving a conflict with an enforced apology removes the symptom while preserving the pattern.
The parent's questions and the school's answers are the working channel of campus safety, the entire reason this appendix exists.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests institutional denial versus threat-responsive handling: whether a reported warning is logged, investigated, and reviewed or minimized as drama and answered with security theater. The claims, that warning signs precede campus violence and that untrained guards are a common false fix, are drawn from de Becker's case observations rather than experimental studies.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: The principal's audit: connecting the fixation to the calendar
assets.question: After a 14-year-old student, Devon Marsh, is stopped outside the gym with a knife, the district interviews Principal Marcella Gomez about what the school knew. Was the school prepared, in denial, or something in between?
assets.subject_baseline: Principal Marcella Gomez has run Westbrook Middle School for six years and keeps a personal, anecdotal memory of students; she calls Devon one of her favorites. She runs a caring office where every student knows they can come to her, and she has never filed a behavioral-threat referral in her tenure, preferring to handle things herself, quietly.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 0:00-0:10: Marcella describes Devon warmly, isolated, quiet, respectful, and volunteers that he loves those war movies and the shooter games he plays with his older cousin, and that he draws soldiers and explosions in every notebook. 0:11-0:24: Asked if anyone connected these interests to anything, she says he never threatened anyone and that he told her he wanted to look strong, and she believed him; her hands rest open on the table. 0:25-0:38: Confronted with the three-week pattern, Devon's drawings growing specifically violent after a discipline incident, his statement to a substitute that the school would pay, and his silent hallway following of the student he blamed, she says she didn't see it like that, she saw a boy who needed a friend. 0:39-0:50: Asked about the date, she pauses: March 14, the day he was held back two years ago; he said the school took his year. Her voice drops and she removes her glasses.
assets.interrogation_transcript: ANALYST: 'What did the school know about Devon before March 14?' MARCELLA: 'That he was struggling. Quiet. He drew constantly, always soldiers, fires. I thought it was a phase.' ANALYST: 'Did anyone log his statement that the school would pay?' MARCELLA: 'A substitute mentioned it. I asked Devon, and he said he was just frustrated and didn't mean it. I believed him. He said he wanted to look strong.' ANALYST: 'Why March 14?' MARCELLA: 'He was held back in March, two years ago. He told me that day that the school took his year from him. I'm just connecting that now.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Denial with a caring mask. The school possessed the documented warning materials, sustained fascination with violent imagery, isolation, the school-will-pay statement, and the anniversary date of his humiliation, and framed all of it as a boy who needed a friend, never logging a single piece. Marcella did not lack affection; she lacked the prediction posture, and her belief that he just wanted to look strong is the book's denial in its most sympathetic form: a caring adult converting an escalation into a phase.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: (1) Baseline: handle things myself, quietly tells the auditor where the institution's knowledge lives, in one warm memory, unlogged and unshared, which is fragile by design. (2) The log shows the data was present: the escalating war imagery, the statement to a substitute, the hallway following, and the calendar coincidence of March 14; each is a pre-incident indicator, and none entered a file. (3) The decisive move is the date: Devon's humiliation anniversary landed on the day of the attempt, meaning the school's own records could have caught the pattern if anyone had been reading threats as information. (4) Marcella's final sentence, I'm just connecting that now, is the audit's answer: the connection was available and unperformed, and the caring framing, a boy who needed a friend, is precisely what made the quiet denial airtight. Verdict: not malicious, not prepared; the school's love was real and its record-keeping was the failure.
distractors: Fully prepared: the school noticed Devon's isolation, kept him close, and gave him a trusted adult, which prevented him from acting sooner.
Deliberately concealing a known risk to protect the school's reputation.
Over-reaction after the fact: a boy's drawings and a muffled the-school-will-pay are normal adolescent venting.
key_concepts: Officials often describe a violent student after the fact as quiet, sweet, and a good student, the denial vocabulary the book warns about.
A sustained fascination with violent media and violent imagery is among the warning signs the book cites for at-risk youth.
In the book's hypothetical list of the hundred most significant influences preceding teen violence, an addiction to media products appears, with alcohol and drugs rated higher.
Warning signs of youth violence are usually observable by several people before any incident.
The destruction of a child's belief that he has purpose and value is named among the saddest consequences described in the book's account of violent young people.
A child whose primary caregiver delivers both praise and brutality is torn between the two identifications.
Goleman's Emotional Intelligence describes seven key abilities most beneficial for human beings, beginning with the ability to motivate ourselves.
An incident that is never logged is an incident the institution can never learn from; information without process is memory.
The date of a humiliation can be as predictive as the humiliation itself, because events carry relationships to other events.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the denial cascade inside a caring institution: known warning materials, violent fixation, a verbal threat, and an anniversary date, were absorbed as personality rather than read as information. The youth-violence indicators are de Becker's case-based and interview-based observations, not validated screening tools, and the audit treats the missed referral as the central failure.
assets.visual_frame_description: A district conference room with a laptop running the school's disciplinary archive; Principal Marcella Gomez sits across from the district analyst with a stack of Devon Marsh's notebooks beside the water pitcher. The player sees Devon's drawings flicker across a side screen as Marcella narrates, dated and tagged, while the March 14 file lands on the table with a thud.
assets.player_mission: Audit what Westbrook Middle School knew about Devon before March 14 and decide whether the school was prepared, in denial, or something in between. Compare the principal's baseline habits, the timed interview log, and the transcript, then deliver the district's verdict.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: The school-board battle: from security theater to prediction practice
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests the appendix's core demand, that parents' questions force schools to convert from reaction (guards and detectors) to prediction (a trained reporting-and-assessment culture). The book's campus and workplace cases show warning signs observable by several people being ignored, and the frequent remedy for pressure, hiring guards, is exactly the false resolution this battle asks the player to reject.
assets.stage_1_observation: The district board chamber at 7 p.m. After a series of threats at three schools, Superintendent Omar Lind presents the plan: two additional guards per campus, hall-pass quotas, and a walk-through metal detector for the high school. Board members nod; the district's safety director is absent; the plan's only mention of students is a dress-code confiscation policy for violent-themed clothing. One parent, Nadia Kim, raises her hand and reads from a notebook: the anonymous tip line has gone unanswered for six months, zero threat assessments have been logged in three years, and the newly hired guards have no training in threat evaluation; they were hired to watch doors. The player watches from the audience and must judge the plan.
assets.stage_1_question: Which single feature of Superintendent Lind's plan shows it is security theater rather than a prediction practice?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The dead anonymous tip line, the one channel through which the book's several people in a position to observe warning signs could actually feed an assessment, is the giveaway: the plan spends money on doors and dress codes while leaving the information pipeline unattended. The guards have no threat-evaluation training, and no threat assessments have been logged in three years, so even the signals that are reported vanish into a six-month-old voicemail. Hiring more guards without supervision or assessment duties is the exact false resolution the book describes: everyone sighs and feels the matter has been addressed, while the incidents the students already know about stay uncollected.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The board recesses for a closed safety session and asks the player to propose the motion for the new policy. Choose the motion that turns the district toward prediction instead of theater.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Move the motion that builds the reporting-and-assessment pipeline: staff in every building trained to log and escalate observations (threats, fixations, drawings, statements to substitutes), a working anonymous tip channel answered within 24 hours, an assessment team that interviews the student, the family, and witnesses before deciding, and a standing semester review of logged incidents, with the guards redeployed to support the process rather than replace it. Explicitly reject the dress-code confiscation as a misread of the problem: the issue is never the imagery on a T-shirt but the information about behavior that no one was collecting.
key_concepts: The typical response to pressure for security is to hire guards, but guards without training or supervision create only the feeling of being addressed.
Warning signs are most often observable by several people before an incident, so the reporting channel is the institution's first instrument.
A fascination with violent media is among the warning signs the book cites for young people at risk of violence.
In the book's hypothetical list of influences preceding teen violence, an addiction to media products appears below alcohol and drugs.
A dead reporting channel is the institutional equivalent of denial: the data exists and is not collected.
The seven abilities Goleman describes as most beneficial, including motivating oneself and managing one's own emotions, are the skills a school intervention can grow.
Prediction must be followed by preparation; a threat-assessment process is preparation that exists before the event.
Sound assessment interviews the student and witnesses rather than interpreting drawings in isolation.
The summit of the book's method is to treat every warning as information and let information drive supervision.
Parents asking their child's school the right questions is the appendix's stated purpose: the questions force the reporting culture into existence.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the conversion from reaction to prediction: rejecting extra guards and dress-code rules in favor of a working reporting-and-assessment pipeline, the mechanism by which warning signs reach people trained to weigh them. The remedy is the book's own prescription drawn from campus and workplace cases, build the channel that collects observable signs, and it is presented as case-based advice about institutional preparation rather than validated policy research.
assets.visual_frame_description: A board chamber with the superintendent's PowerPoint on the wall, two guards in new uniforms standing at the doors, and a parent's notebook open on the lectern showing the unanswered tip line. The player sits in the audience, and the plan's line items glow and dim as the flaw-hunting mode activates.
assets.player_mission: Judge Superintendent Lind's security plan for signs of theater rather than prediction, then propose the motion that builds a reporting-and-assessment pipeline. Identify the single dead channel that betrays the plan, and win the vote with the motion that collects warning signs.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)
